{{Short description|Algebraic plane curve}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[Image:Devils curve a=0.8 b=1.svg|right|thumb|Devil's curve for {{nowrap|''a'' {{=}} 0.8}} and {{nowrap|''b'' {{=}} 1}}.]]}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[Image:Devils curve a=0.0-1.0 b=1.svg|right|thumb|Devil's curve with <math>a</math> ranging from 0 to 1 and {{nowrap|''b'' {{=}} 1}} (with the curve colour going from blue to red).]]}}
In [[geometry]], a '''Devil's curve''', also known as the '''Devil on Two Sticks''', is a [[curve]] defined in the [[Cartesian plane]] by an equation of the form<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DevilsCurve.html | title=Devil's Curve |website=Wolfram MathWorld}}</ref>

<math display=block> y^4 - b^2y^2 = x^4 - a^2x^2 </math> i.e. a Quartic, in terms of x and y.

The [[polar equation]] of this curve is of the form

<math display=block>r = \sqrt{\frac{b^2 \sin^2\theta-a^2 \cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta-\cos^2\theta}} = \sqrt{\frac{b^2 -a^2 \cot^2\theta}{1-\cot^2\theta}}</math>

Devil's curves were discovered in 1750 by [[Gabriel Cramer]], who studied them extensively.<ref>Introduction a l'analyse des lignes courbes algébriques, p. 19 (Genova, 1750).</ref> 

The name comes from the shape its central [[lemniscate]] takes when graphed. The shape is named after the juggling game [[diabolo]], which was named after the Devil<ref>{{cite web|title=Diabolo Patent|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US822628|access-date=16 July 2013}}</ref> and which involves two sticks, a string, and a spinning prop in the likeness of the lemniscate.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.2dcurves.com/quartic/quarticd.html |title=devil's curve |last=Wassenaar |first=Jan  |website=www.2dcurves.com |access-date=2018-02-26}}</ref>

For <math> |b|>|a| </math>, the central lemniscate, often called hour-glass, is horizontal,
For <math> |b|<|a| </math> it is vertical. If <math> |b|=|a| </math>, the shape becomes a circle.
The vertical hour-glass intersects the y-axis at <math> -b,0,b </math> . The horizontal hour-glass intersects the x-axis at <math> -a,0,a </math> and for the four turning points, for this hour-glass,
<math display=block> \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(a^2-2x^2)}{y(b^2-2y^2)}=0 </math> giving:
<math display=block> x=+/- \frac{\sqrt2}{2}a </math>

Total Area of horizontal hour-glass 
<math display=block>\approx 2.8284\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{b^2-\sqrt{-4a^2x^2+b^4+4x^4}}\,dx </math>

==Electric Motor Curve==

A special case of the Devil's curve occurs at <math>\frac{a^2}{b^2}=\frac{25}{24}</math>, where the curve is called the '''electric motor curve'''.<ref>[https://ia801606.us.archive.org/28/items/MathematicalModels-/HMartynCundy_APRollett-mathematicalModels-oxfordClarendonPress1961.pdf Mathematical Models, p. 71 (Cundy and Rollet. 1961)]</ref> It is defined by an equation of the form

<math display=block>y^2(y^2-96) = x^2(x^2-100)</math>

The name of the special case comes from the middle shape's resemblance to the coils of wire, which rotate from forces exerted by magnets surrounding it.
